opener.heading: Week 2: Nursery Rhymes & Rhythm 🎶
about: Every rhyme she knows is a machine for keeping time, and this week she takes them apart. She fills five shakers and lines them up quietest to loudest, drops an egg off a wall she built herself, counts five ducks down to none and back again, and hits an upturned saucepan once for every piece of a word. The rhymes stay the same all week. Her job with them changes each morning.

No holiday lands in this stretch, so the week runs on its own thread and the gear piles up as it goes. Five sealed shakers on Friday, a kitchen drum kit on Monday, a hat and a flag on Thursday, and by the last afternoon the whole house is marching a route Azlyn drew on a sheet of paper on the floor. Three afternoons end with your phone recording her singing, one of them a song she writes about Kreston. Back those up before Thursday.
azlyn: The beat inside a word. AZ-LYN is two hits, SPA-GHET-TI is four, and she hears the pieces long before she can name them.
Loud and quiet on purpose. Scarf up is loud, scarf down is quiet, and she is the one holding the scarf.
Counting down, and starting again from one. Five ducks to none, ten in the bed to one, five buns off a tray.
Calling it before it happens. She says cracked or not cracked out loud, then opens her hand over the tray and finds out.
Patterns she can hear. Spoon, cup, spoon, cup, and the gap where you took one out of the middle.
you: Why she only has one volume, and it is loud
Why the rhymes she loves are all a bit gruesome
Why she wants the same rhyme forty times
Rhythm and reading are more connected than they look
Why a wind-down object works better than a wind-down instruction
Counting words come long before counting means anything
Why moving together matters more than moving
shopping: Eggs, at least 4, boiled Friday night and left to go cold
Oats or a bag of frozen peas, for the ducks
Milk and a cinnamon stick, for the bedtime drink
Five bread rolls, if you want real buns in the bun shop
5 small plastic bottles or yogurt pots with lids
A large cookie tin, or any large empty can
A plastic tub with a lid
A tray and a baking tray
Plain paper, a stack, plus the biggest single sheet in the house
A glue stick, or flour and water paste in a saucer
A metal skewer, or a pencil sharpened to a point (adult only)
A pencil and a tape measure
An old magazine to push the skewer down onto
Spoons: 2 wooden, 1 metal, 1 teaspoon, and 8 of any kind for the pattern row
A blue dish towel or a second scarf for the pond
A dish towel to stuff inside a drum
An old towel to line the tray
A pillowcase or a tote bag
A blanket, and Kreston's own blanket
A spare duvet, or a mattress on the floor
Books or small boxes, 6–8, to build Humpty's wall
A flashlight with fresh batteries, and spares
A watch for the rhyme bag
Your phone, with room on it to record
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 7 months this week. He reaches across his own body for something on the far side, moves a toy from one hand to the other to get a better look at it, and babbles in long strings with a beat running through them.

days.title: Shakers and Spoons
days.prepTonight: Stand five empty pots and their lids by the dry-goods cupboard with the packing tape and a marker, and boil four eggs for tomorrow, left in the fridge to go cold.

opening.title: Listening to the Cupboard
opening.need: the dry-goods cupboard, open · 1 metal spoon · 5 empty pots with lids.
steps: Sit her in front of the open cupboard and let her tap the packages with the back of the spoon. Rice, pasta, lentils, cereal, sugar. Each answers in a different voice.
Shut your eyes and let her tap one for you to name. Get one wrong on purpose.
Line up the five pots and let her decide which package goes in which. You label them at 9:15.

main.title: The Shaker Set
materials: 5 small plastic bottles or yogurt pots with lids
1 sheet of paper rolled into a funnel
steps: Roll the paper into a cone, tape the seam and stand it in the first pot. She pours, you hold. Some goes on the table and that is the price.
Fill each pot a third full. A pot packed to the lid makes almost no sound, so let her overfill one and hear it.
Tape every lid all the way round twice and press the seams flat. Write the contents on the side of each pot in marker.
Shake them one at a time with her eyes shut. Ask her to point at the loudest before she opens them.
Stand all five along the table, quietest to loudest. Move them as often as she wants.
Number the bases one to five once she settles. She comes back to this line at 4:15.
main.tip: The sugar shaker sounds like rain and she will lose interest inside a minute. Keep it. It is the quiet end of the line, and the only instrument in this afternoon's whisper verse.

outside.title: Tapping the Railings
paras: Take a wooden spoon out with you and tap what you pass. Railings ring and hold the note, fence posts thud and stop dead, a trash can booms, a brick wall gives back nothing. January metal is cold enough that she will want gloves on and then off again to feel it. Let her find the loudest thing on the street and stay at it.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and reaching across his own body for things on the far side. Sit him back from the table with a wooden spoon and an upturned saucepan, and put the spoon down on his far side so he has to cross over for it. Keep the small pots away from him. Shake one by his left ear, then his right, and watch him turn toward a sound he cannot see.

second.title: Loud Song, Quiet Song
second.intro: The shakers have their order. This afternoon Azlyn plays one rhyme four ways and decides which way comes next.
materials: Your phone, to record the last run
steps: Sit everyone in a ring, shakers in the middle, saucepan by your knee, scarf in Azlyn's hand.
Pick a rhyme the whole house knows. Twinkle, Twinkle or The Wheels on the Bus. Sing it through once with a shaker each for you and Azlyn.
Loud version. Saucepan on the beat, cardboard tube as a megaphone, pasta and lentils flat out. One verse, and one verse alone.
Quiet version. Sugar shaker on its own, everyone whispering, heads close together. She drops her voice to match yours.
Fast, then slow. Slow is the hard one, and one verse at half speed lasts longer than either of you expects.
Hand her the scarf. Scarf up is loud, scarf down is quiet, and she runs the band. Follow her even when she flips it every two words.
Record the last run. Play it back once, then again with everyone singing on top of it.
second.tip: The whisper verse works better if you get smaller. Sit on the floor, lean in, let your voice go thin.

alternatives: Two shakers and one rhyme, sat on the sofa.
March round the kitchen table with the saucepan and nothing else.
Sort the shakers by what is inside instead of how loud they are.
Sing the same rhyme in a squeaky voice, a growly voice and a whisper.
outAgain: A cafe with cake, a window seat and a street to watch
The neighborhood park, for twenty minutes of running
The bakery counter, and let her choose for tomorrow
A friend's house, if anyone can take an afternoon of shakers
Home, with the shakers in the bath

aroundWorld.title: Lullabies Everywhere 🌙
paras: Every country puts its children to sleep with a song, and the songs resemble each other more than the languages do. Wales has Suo Gân, sung on the same slow fall as the Japanese Itsuki no Komoriuta. Swahili families sing Lala salama, sleep safe. Researchers played babies lullabies from cultures they had never heard, and the babies settled to those too.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Warm milk with a cinnamon stick, the bedtime drink in a great many houses. Give Azlyn hers in the same cup all week and sing one lullaby that is not in English.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Lullabies the world over share a slow, falling tune, which is why a song in a language she has never met still works on her.

days.krestonPM: He is 7 months and babbling in long strings now, ba-ba-ba and da-da-da-da, a rhythm section of his own. Sit him at the outside of the ring on your lap or with a folded blanket behind him, back from the shakers in the middle. He answers singing sooner than talking, so leave a gap at the end of each verse and see whether he fills it. Keep the loud verse short and watch his face while it runs.

insight.headline: Why she only has one volume, and it is loud.
paras: Azlyn can do quiet on request and hold it for about four seconds. The holding is the hard part, and it runs on the same slow-growing machinery as waiting her turn and stopping halfway down the hall. Volume control is inhibition, and a three-year-old has a thin supply. She gets better at it by practicing the switch rather than by being asked for less noise. Handing her the loud verse first and the whisper verse second gives her both ends to feel in her own throat a minute apart. The scarf makes her the one calling the change, and running the switch builds it faster than obeying it.

days.safety: Dried rice, lentils and pasta on the floor are a choking hazard for a 7-month-old, and a taped lid can still come off. Tape all the way round each pot, check every seal before it goes down, and keep the small pots away from Kreston.

days.title: Humpty Dumpty's Wall
days.prepTonight: The four eggs are boiled and cold in the fridge. Fold an old towel into a baking tray beside them, and stand the books for the wall by the kitchen door.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Quiet End of a Loud Day

opening.title: Drawing on the Eggs
opening.need: 4 cold boiled eggs · 1 permanent marker · 1 egg cup.
steps: Fetch the four boiled eggs you left cold in the fridge last night, then hand her the marker and one egg at a time. Faces, hats, whatever she wants. Marker takes a minute to dry on a shell, so hold each one by the ends.
Say the rhyme together while she draws. She will reach the line about nobody putting him together again and look up at you.
Stand the best one in the egg cup on the windowsill. Nobody touches him before 9:15.

main.title: The Egg Drop Record
materials: 4 hard-boiled eggs, boiled last night and cooled, or boiled at 8:00 and cooled fast in a bowl of cold water
1 old towel to line the tray
6–8 books or small boxes to build the wall
steps: Line the tray with the folded towel and set it on the kitchen floor. She stacks the books into a wall beside it.
Sit Humpty on top and say the rhyme once with him up there.
First drop from ankle height, straight into the tray. Measure with the tape and write the number down before she opens her hand.
Ask her to call it before every drop: cracked or not cracked. Write her answer beside the number. Knee height next, then hip.
Take the towel out for the last egg and drop it on the bare tray from ankle height. It breaks where it was safe five minutes ago.
Read the paper back to her. Her numbers, her guesses, and the one that caught her out.
main.tip: Let her hold the egg and let her be the one who opens her hand. An egg she drops herself is her experiment.

outside.title: The Low Wall Balance
paras: Find a low garden wall, a curb edge or the flat top of a step and walk her along it holding one hand. She sits at the far end with her legs over and says the rhyme from up there, then jumps into your hands. January stone keeps its frost all morning in the shade, so put your own hand flat on the top first.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and has started dropping food over the side of the high chair and leaning out to look. Same experiment, cheaper equipment. Sit him where he can see the tray for three or four drops. Then give him an egg cup on his own tray and pick it up eight times without comment.

second.title: The Mended Egg
second.intro: Humpty's shell is still sitting on the tray. She glues him back together this afternoon, the one thing the rhyme insists nobody could do.
materials: The cracked shells from this morning
1 sheet of thick paper or card
A glue stick, or flour and water paste in a saucer
1 pencil to draw the egg outline
steps: Draw a big egg outline on the card in pencil, or let her draw it and go over her line so she can see it.
Tip the shell onto a sheet of paper and let her press it small with the back of a spoon. Fingers work too.
Mix the paste if you are using it: two tablespoons of flour, water stirred in until it runs like cream.
Cover a small patch of the egg at a time. Paste the whole outline at once and it dries before she has filled a third of it.
She presses the shell down. Let her go outside the line and leave gaps, and keep your hands off.
Crayon in the rest: the wall underneath, the king's horses, a face on the shell.
Write her title along the bottom in her own words, then put it up high to dry.
second.tip: The shell runs out near the top and she will notice. Crayon fills the gap, and the picture is better for one bald patch.

alternatives: Shells into a bowl of water and stir. That is the whole activity.
Draw Humpty on a flattened box and glue nothing.
Paint the shells today and glue them tomorrow.
Sort the pieces into big, medium and tiny on three saucers.
outAgain: A bus ride to nowhere in particular, upstairs at the front
The park, for the low wall she balanced on this morning
Indoor playground if the weather has gone sideways
A walk to look at real brick walls and count the courses
The store for eggs, since you are four down
days.krestonPM: Keep him at the table and off the shells. Stick a long strip of masking tape to his high chair tray and let him work it loose. At 7 months he moves a thing from one hand to the other for a better angle. On the bus he wants the window, so face him out on your lap and name the stops.

insight.headline: Why the rhymes she loves are all a bit gruesome.
paras: Humpty smashes. The cradle falls out of the tree, baby and all. Three mice lose their tails to a carving knife. Azlyn asks for these on repeat and then sleeps fine, because a rhyme keeps a small disaster inside a shape that never alters. She knows the ending before it arrives, so the fall frightens her the way a slide frightens her, with the floor already in view. Rehearsing an alarming thing at a safe distance is how she works out its real size. Dropping the egg herself went further again: she caused the crack, she stood over it, and it turned out smaller than the rhyme makes it sound.

days.safety: Shell fragments have sharp edges and are exactly the size Kreston puts in his mouth. Keep the tray and the glued sheet up high, sweep the floor before he goes down, and wipe egg off a hard floor straight away because it is slippery.

days.title: Five Little Ducks
days.prepTonight: Flatten a cereal box for the ducks, stand the laundry basket upside down in the living room, and put a pillowcase beside it.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Over the Hill and Far Away

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: One Last Rhyme from the Bag

opening.title: Making the Five Ducks
opening.need: 1 flattened cereal box · scissors (adult only) · crayons · 5 clothespins.
steps: Draw five duck shapes on the plain side of the box. Rough ovals with a beak on the front will do.
You cut, she colors. Give each one something different, and let her choose which is the mother duck.
Clip a clothespin to the bottom of each so they stand up. Line all five along the table and count them twice.

main.title: Over the Hill and Far Away
materials: 1 cereal box, for cutting five duck shapes
5 clothespins to stand the ducks up
1 upturned laundry basket or a sofa cushion
1 blue dish towel or scarf for the pond
steps: Turn the laundry basket upside down in the middle of the floor for the hill. Spread the dish towel in front of it for the pond and tape the corners flat.
Stand all five ducks on the pond. Run a strip of masking tape across the floor behind the hill to mark where far away starts.
Sing the first verse. On the line about only four coming back, she takes one duck over the hill and stands it on the tape.
Count what is left on the pond after each verse, touching each duck as its number comes. She does the quacking, all of it.
Keep going down to none, and sit in the quiet of an empty pond before the last verse.
Mother duck calls and all five come back over together. She carries them, and she will want the whole thing again, so do it again.
main.tip: Put the vanished ducks somewhere she can see the tops of. A duck gone for good gets checked on halfway through the next verse.

outside.title: Walking in a Duck Line
paras: Walk the block in single file. She goes first as the mother duck, everyone behind her waddles, and at each corner the person at the back moves to the front. Count off before you set out and count again at home to see whether anybody went over the hill and far away. January puddles have ice at the rim and she will stamp every one of them.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months. Prop him with a cushion on the far side of the hill, facing the basket, so every duck rises over the top and drops out of sight. Gone and back is the funniest thing available to him this month. On the duck line he babbles back at the quacking, so leave him a gap between verses.

second.title: The Rhyme Bag
second.intro: One object per rhyme goes into a pillowcase, and the bag decides what the house sings.
materials: 6–8 household objects, one per rhyme: a spoon, a card star, a rolled sock, a watch, a plastic cup, an egg cup, one of the cardboard ducks
1 sheet of card and 1 marker for picture labels
steps: Gather the objects and give each one its rhyme out loud. The spoon ran away with the dish, the mouse ran up the watch, the sock is Diddle Diddle Dumpling.
Draw a picture label on card for each one, rough and fast, and lay it beside its object.
Everything into the pillowcase. She reaches in without looking, feels about, pulls one out.
Whatever comes out, the whole house sings it. No skipping and no swapping.
Let her guess by feel before she looks, one guess out loud.
Once the bag is empty, lay the objects in the order they arrived and sing the set through as one medley.
Refill it and hand her the bag. She runs it and you sing whatever she pulls.
second.tip: Slip in one object with no rhyme attached, a shoe or an apple, and let her invent something when it comes out. Her version goes in the bag with the rest.

alternatives: Three objects, one bag, sat on the bed.
Line the objects up and let her set the order you sing them in.
Hide the five ducks round the room and sing a verse for each one found.
Draw the labels and stop there; the bag can wait until tomorrow.
outAgain: Feeding the ducks at the pond, with oats or defrosted peas rather than bread
The park, for the swings and a shorter walk home
A long loop with the stroller if the pond is frozen over
The playground with the tunnel, out of the wind
A drive to somewhere with water, and stay in the warm car
days.krestonPM: Wrap him well for the pond. At 7 months a bank full of birds moving against gray water is the biggest thing he has been shown all week. Keep him off the ground at the edge. Twenty minutes in that cold is plenty.

insight.headline: Why she wants the same rhyme forty times.
paras: The fortieth Five Little Ducks is not the same event for her that it is for you. The first few passes take everything she has to follow the tune. Once the tune runs on its own, she has room to hear the words. Once the words are free, she notices the number dropping by one every verse, and after that she finds the joke in the last line. Repetition buys her the spare capacity to attend to the next layer down. Research on toddler word learning keeps landing in the same place: a few books read over and over beat a wide rotation for what stays. Sing it again.

days.safety: The clothespins and the small rhyme-bag objects are choke-sized, so they come off the floor before Kreston does. Puddle ice this month is thin, so keep her off the frozen edge of anything deeper than her boot. If you take the pond option this afternoon, hold her hand at the water, scatter the food from well back, and stay between both children and the bank.

days.title: The Beat in Every Word
days.prepTonight: Put a large tin, a plastic tub, an empty cereal box and a saucepan by the table, and dig out two wooden spoons and the packing tape.

opening.title: The Spoon and the Saucepan
steps: Turn the pan upside down on the floor between you and give her the spoon.
Say her name in pieces and hit the pan once for each piece. AZ-LYN, two hits. KRES-TON, two. BROOK-LYN, two.
Let her do yours, then let her do words that are not names. Hit whatever she says, however many pieces she reckons it has.

main.title: The Kitchen Drum Kit
materials: 1 large cookie tin or a large empty can
1 dish towel, to mute one drum
steps: Line the tin, the tub, the cereal box and the saucepan along the floor and tape their bases down so they stop traveling.
Hit each one and let her say which is high and which is low. Stuff the dish towel into the box, hit it again, and she hears the same drum go dull.
Names first, one hit per piece. Everyone in the house, then the neighbors, then the cat, then people she has invented.
Move on to food for longer words. BREAD is one hit. BA-NA-NA is three. SPA-GHET-TI is four and she will want that one over and over.
Play a rhyme line by line. TWIN-KLE TWIN-KLE LIT-TLE STAR, one hit per piece. Number the drums one to four in marker if she starts calling for a particular one.
She plays something short and you copy it back, then you play and she copies. Keep them to three hits.
main.tip: Say the word out loud while you hit it, every time. She is matching her mouth to her hand.

outside.title: Stamping Out the Names
paras: Walk the street and stamp what you pass. GATE is one stamp. LAMP-POST is two. FIRE HY-DRANT is three. Frozen puddles sit in the shade all day this month and a stamp on thin ice gives her a crack and a splinter pattern. She names the thing, she stamps it, and you take her count.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and his babble has gone into long strings, ba-ba-ba-ba, each with a beat in it. Sit him well back from the kit with a plastic tub turned over and let him slap it flat handed. Answer him in his own rhythm: he gives you four, you give four back. He will wait for your turn.

second.title: The Pattern You Can Hear
second.intro: She lays a row of objects along the floor, gives each one a sound, and plays the row left to right.
materials: 1 long strip of paper, or a line of masking tape on the floor
The drum kit from this morning
steps: Run the masking tape in a long line down the floor, or lay the paper strip out. That is the row.
Start it off yourself. Spoon, cup, spoon, cup, spoon, cup, saying each one aloud. Ask her what comes next and wait through the silence.
Give every object a sound. Spoon is a tap on the tin, cup is a slap on the tub, sock is silence. She will fill the row with socks.
Play the row left to right, pointing at each object as its sound comes. Then again, faster. Then again with her pointing and you playing.
Hand the row over. She builds the next one and you play it back, note for note, including the row that is seven socks and a spoon.
Take one object out of the middle of a repeating row and play it again. Ask her what went missing.
Photograph the last row before you clear it up, then let her play it from the photo.
second.tip: Leave her patterns alone. A row that breaks its own rule is a row she made a decision about.

alternatives: Six objects, one short row, done on the sofa.
Clap her name and yours back and forth and stop there.
Lay the row outside on the path with sticks and stones instead.
Bang the drums while she conducts with the scarf from Friday.
outAgain: The neighborhood park, for the swings and the bark chippings
The riverside path, if the puddles from this morning held
A walk to mail something and stamp the whole way there
The corner store, and let her carry one thing home
Indoor playground if the cold has beaten everybody
days.krestonPM: He goes on the row. Put him at one end with a cushion behind him and let his sock be the last object in the pattern. At 7 months he reaches across his own middle, so set a spoon past his opposite shoulder and watch him twist over for it. Every time you play the row, end on him.

insight.headline: Rhythm and reading are more connected than they look.
paras: Clapping BA-NA-NA into three pieces is reading practice, three years before she meets a letter. Reading asks her to hear that a word breaks into parts, hold those parts in order, and match them onto shapes on a page. The hearing comes first and beat is how children get at it. Preschoolers who can keep time with a steady pulse score higher on the sound-awareness tests that predict later reading, and the link survives once you account for age and vocabulary. Every rhyme sung in this house since Friday has run that machinery. The drums make it loud enough for her to catch herself doing it.

days.safety: A saucepan banged at close range is loud enough to hurt a 7-month-old's ears. Keep Kreston an arm's length back from the kit, give him his own quiet tub, and stop the session before it turns into hitting for volume. Wooden spoons swing at exactly his head height.

days.title: Twinkle, Twinkle
days.prepTonight: Check the flashlight batteries, and keep three or four paper cups back from the recycling.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Star Cup and Two Books

opening.title: Finding the Darkest Corner
opening.need: 1 flashlight · every door in the house · her.
steps: Walk her round with the flashlight off, shutting doors and pulling curtains as you go. Stand in each room for a slow count of ten and let your eyes adjust.
Ask her which one is darkest. Bathrooms and the cupboard under the stairs tend to win.
Test the winner. Shine the flashlight at the ceiling and watch the circle arrive. Leave those curtains shut for the rest of the day.

main.title: The Star Cup
materials: 3–4 paper cups, or squares of dark card
1 metal skewer, or a sharpened pencil (adult only)
1 old magazine to push down onto
A room that goes dark with the door shut
steps: Sit her at the table with a cup and the marker and let her dot a pattern over the base and the sides. Ten or fifteen dots is plenty. A hundred dots makes a lamp.
Stand the cup on the old magazine and push the skewer through each dot. You do all the pushing, she counts them off as they go.
Make a second cup with a different pattern and let her name them both.
Take the cups and the flashlight into the dark room. Flashlight pointing up, cup over the end of it, a strip of tape round the join if the fit is loose.
Light off. Her stars land on the ceiling and travel when you tilt the flashlight. Lie on your backs underneath and sing the rhyme.
Hand her the flashlight. It will go across the wall, the floor and your face.
main.tip: Give the stars some distance. A cup held close to the ceiling throws a tight patch. Down at floor level the same cup throws a sky.

outside.title: The Sleeping Street
paras: Walk the usual route hunting for things that have shut down for winter. Buds on the bare twigs are sealed tight and will sit there until March. Ask her where the birds go at night, take her answer at face value, then go and look at the places she might be right about. The light goes not long after five this month.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months. Lay him on his back in the dark room for five minutes with the star cup on. He follows a slow-moving light across a whole ceiling now, and he will reach across his own body after one that crosses over him. Keep the beam off his face.

second.title: Kreston's Own Song
second.intro: Twinkle, Twinkle carries a tune the whole house already owns, so the words can be about anything. Azlyn picks what goes in the verse, and she picks her brother.
materials: Paper and crayons for the picture that goes with the song
steps: Ask Azlyn what Kreston did today. Write it down as she says it, including the parts that did not happen.
Pick four items off the list. The daft ones survive, and she does the choosing.
Fit them to the tune a line at a time, singing each line the moment you have it so she hears whether it lands. Too many pieces crammed into a line is the usual trouble.
Sing the finished verse twice so she has it in her. Then let her change a word.
Record it on your phone, her singing and you underneath her. One take. Do not ask her for a tidier version.
She draws the picture while the recording plays back. Kreston's blanket goes over her lap, or over him.
Play it to Kreston sat on your knee facing his sister. He will hunt for where the sound comes from and find her face at the end of it.
second.tip: Put the recording somewhere you will find it again. A three-year-old singing a song she made up about her brother disappears into a phone.

alternatives: New words to Twinkle about the cat, the bath or dinner.
Draw the picture and skip the recording.
Star cup and flashlight on the ceiling for an hour, nothing else.
Sing the old words in four voices and let her pick a winner.
outAgain: Swimming, and she can sing in the changing room
Indoor playground if the pool is shut or the line is out the door
The library, a day early
A warm cafe and a window, if nobody has the energy for a pool
Home, with the star cup and the curtains shut
days.krestonPM: He swims too. At 7 months he sits supported in the water and reaches for anything floating within a hand's reach, so take an upturned cup in and let him chase it. Your hands stay on him the whole time he is in the water. Sing the star song at him in there, where the tiled echo turns your voice into something new. Twenty minutes, then out before he cools.

insight.headline: Why a wind-down object works better than a wind-down instruction.
paras: Telling a lit-up three-year-old to calm down hands her the entire job. She has to notice the state, want it changed, and run the change herself, and she can manage about one of those on a good evening. An object takes the work off her. The star cup comes out, the big light goes off, the same song plays, and the sequence does the slowing for her. She has met that order often enough that the first step predicts the rest, so her body starts settling at the cup rather than at the bed. You already run this with the bath and the books. The cup joins the end of the line tonight.

days.safety: The skewer is adult-only and goes back in the drawer between cups, not on the table. If the flashlight takes button cells, tape the compartment shut; a swallowed button battery burns through a child's throat within hours. At the pool, Kreston stays in arm's reach in the water, every second.

days.title: Ten in the Bed
days.prepTonight: Gather ten soft toys into a basket, pull a spare duvet or a mattress onto the bedroom floor, and keep one more cereal box and a shoebox back.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Counting the Doors to Number Ten

opening.title: Lining Up the Bears
opening.need: 10 soft toys · 1 blanket · a stretch of floor.
steps: Tip out the basket of ten soft toys you gathered last night and let her line all ten along the edge of the blanket, in whatever order she wants.
Count the row together, touching each one as the number comes out. Let her tell you their names and write them down.
Ask her who is going over the edge first. Whoever she picks goes on the end until 9:15.

main.title: Roll Over, Roll Over
materials: A bed, or a mattress or duvet on the floor
Paper and a marker for the countdown
2 pillows as a barrier at the edge
steps: Put the mattress or the duvet on the floor, or use the bed with both pillows packed along the open side. Everybody goes over an edge this morning, so the edge wants to be low.
Lay the ten toys along the blanket in the order she made, with her at one end of the row.
Sing the verse. On "roll over" everyone rolls, toys included, and the one on the end goes off the side.
Count who is left after every verse, touching each one, then write the new number on the paper. Nine. Eight. Seven.
Let her say the number that opens the next verse. She will skip one, so count the row again and find out who is right.
The last verse has one left and nobody to roll into. Sit in that, then let her throw all ten back on and start again.
main.tip: The fallen toys land in a heap and she will want them back up. Keep the heap where she can see it growing.

outside.title: Counting the Doors to Number Ten
paras: Walk down one side of the street reading the house numbers out loud. Find number one and walk as far as number ten, and let her spot each numeral on the gate before you say it. Odd on one side and even on the other will bother her, and it is worth crossing the road to sort out.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months. Sit him at the foot of the mattress with a cushion behind him and hand him each toy as it comes off the edge. He takes it, turns it over, moves it to his other hand, then drops it. Keep him off the rolling surface.

second.title: The Bun Shop
second.intro: Five Currant Buns in a Baker's Shop wants a shop, a baker and somebody with money in their hand.
materials: 1 cereal box, for five bun circles (or five real bread rolls if you have them)
10 card coins, cut from the same box
steps: Cut five circles from the cereal box and ten coins from what is left. She draws the currants on, as many per bun as she likes.
Set the tray on a low table as the counter and the shoebox behind it as the register. She is the baker, and the shop opens when she says.
Count the buns onto the tray out loud. Five, touching each one.
Sing the verse, walk up with a coin, buy one bun and carry it away. She hands the bun over and puts the coin in the register herself.
After each sale, ask how many are left and let her count the tray from the start. Wait out the recount.
Sell all five, then swap. She counts the coins out of the register one at a time into your hand.
Shut the shop. Count the five coins in your hand and the five buns beside them, and stack both on the tray.
second.tip: Do the buying in real time. A pause between sales, a walk to the door, a knock before you come in. She has to hold the number while the shop waits.

alternatives: Three buns, no coins, no register.
Real rolls, and eat the stock at snack time.
Set the shop up and let her sell to the ten bears instead.
Draw a shop front on a flattened box and stop there.
outAgain: Indoor playground, and the quiet hour before school pickup if there is one
The library, if indoor playground is packed
The park in the cold, for twenty minutes and hot chocolate after
A friend's house, with the rhyme bag in your coat pocket
The indoor play center, if the weather has shut everything else down
days.krestonPM: Indoor playground at 7 months means the baby corner and nothing beyond it. He sits without help now, so put him on the mats with two soft blocks in reach and let the older children run past him. Half an hour, before the noise catches up with him.

insight.headline: Counting words come long before counting means anything.
paras: Azlyn can chant to ten and still not know that the last word she said is the answer. Rote counting arrives first, as a song with numbers in it. The idea underneath, that the number you land on tells you how many there are, takes another year or so and it arrives through touching. One finger on one bear as one word leaves her mouth is the whole bridge, and so is a bun going off the tray and the tray having one fewer on it. Both were in today. Ask her how many and let her recount from one every single time, because starting again from one is the work at three.

days.safety: Ten in the Bed ends with somebody going over the edge. Do it on a mattress on the floor, or pillow the drop side and stay on it. Card coins only; real coins are the classic swallowed object at this age, and Kreston will be under the table hunting for whatever rolled.

days.title: The Marching Band
days.prepTonight: Back up this week's recordings off your phone, find a hat for everybody, put the week's shakers, drums and spoons into one basket, and dig out the biggest sheet of paper in the house.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Up the Hill and Down Again

opening.title: Handing Out the Instruments
opening.need: the week's shakers, drums and spoons in one basket · a hat each.
steps: Put the basket down in the middle of the floor and let her hand the instruments out. She decides who gets what, including what you get.
Hats on. Anything counts: a sun hat, a woolly one, a saucepan.
Everyone plays their own thing at once for thirty seconds, then stops dead the moment she says stop. Do that twice and leave it until 9:15.

main.title: Up the Hill and Down Again
materials: The week's shakers, drums and spoons
1 sheet of paper, 1 wooden spoon and tape, for a flag
steps: Build the hill. Four to six cushions stacked in the middle of the floor, wide enough to walk up and firm enough to stand on at the top.
Tape the sheet of paper to the wooden spoon for a flag. She decides what goes on the flag and she carries it.
Line up behind the flag with the instruments and the hats. March round the room once to get the step going, everyone starting on the same foot.
Sing the Grand Old Duke of York. Up the cushions on "up", down the other side on "down".
Halfway up and halfway down, stop dead on the word and hold it. Hold it longer than feels comfortable. She will ask for it eight times.
Tape Kreston's shaker twice round and check the seal, then bring him into the line for the last two runs.
main.tip: March slower than feels right. Ten thousand men come down that hill at half the speed you would walk it.

outside.title: In Step Round the Block
paras: March the block. Left, right, left, right, called out loud, everyone setting off on the same foot. She loses the step inside twenty paces and finds it again. Halt at each corner and freeze for a count of five. January sidewalks are wet or salted, so drop the calling for a stretch and listen to the boots instead.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and rides this one in the carrier, where the bounce of your step goes straight through him. Babies pick a beat up through the body long before they pick it out by ear. Sing the same four lines the whole way round.

second.title: The Whole House Parade
second.intro: The parade needs a route, and she draws it before anybody marches anywhere.
materials: 1 large sheet of paper for the route map
Masking tape to mark the stops on the floor
Your phone, to record the last run
steps: Spread the big sheet on the floor and draw the downstairs as one long line. Front door, hall, kitchen, living room, back to the door. She adds the rooms you forget.
Mark four or five stops along the line, one per doorway. She picks a rhyme for each stop and you draw a small picture of it on the map.
Tape an X on the floor at each stop so the band knows where to halt.
Run it once with you leading. Play and march between the stops, halt on the X, everyone sings that doorway's rhyme.
Run it again with Azlyn out front and the flag in her hand. She sets the speed, and the speed will be wrong.
Third run, Kreston leads from your hip and Azlyn walks behind him with the drum.
Record the last run on your phone, walking backwards in front of the band. Sit on the floor together and watch it once.
second.tip: Let the route be daft. A parade that goes through the bathroom and out again is a better parade than a sensible one.

alternatives: One stop, one rhyme, the hall and back.
Draw the map today and march it tomorrow.
Parade for an audience of ten soft toys lined up in the hall.
Take the instruments into the yard and march the fence line.
outAgain: The hardware store, for tape, batteries and a look at the paint chips
The park on the way back, for the swings
The corner store, and let her pay
A walk to drop something at a neighbor's door
The library, if the store can wait until tomorrow
days.krestonPM: Take him into the hardware store in the carrier facing out. At 7 months the high shelves, the fluorescent lights and the racket of a big store are work for him, so twenty minutes is enough. Back home he gets his taped shaker for the last parade run, checked once more before it reaches his hands.

insight.headline: Why moving together matters more than moving.
paras: Marching in step with Azlyn does something that dancing on your own round the kitchen does not. Move in time with another person and you both come away more inclined to help each other, and it shows up young. Bounce a fourteen-month-old in time with you and he hands back an object you drop more often than a baby bounced out of time. Four-year-olds show something like it after they have made music together. Shared rhythm reads as belonging, at any age, which is most of what a nursery rhyme has ever been for. Everything sung in this house since Friday has been two or four people locking onto one beat. Today it has hats.

days.safety: Build the hill low and wide, and stay within arm's reach the whole time she is standing on the top. A stack of cushions slides apart under a three-year-old's feet. Tape Kreston's shaker all the way round twice and check the seal every time before it reaches his hands. In the marching line, keep the spoons and shakers clear of his head; in the carrier it sits at swinging height.
